HAVE you ever HEARD of 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗰 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝘅???...🍔

A single McDonald’s Burger can tell you a lot about Global Currency Valuations. 

According to The Economist’s July 2026 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗰 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝘅, the exact same Burger varies wildly in price depending on where you buy it, offering a fascinating snapshot of purchasing power parity (PPP) across 53 countries and the Euro area.

Here is how the Global Menu stacks up:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲:
☑️ Switzerland: $9.04 (45% higher than the U.S. benchmark) 
   ☑️ Uruguay: $8.94 
   ☑️ Norway: $8.05 
   ☑️ Euro Area: $7.08 (8th overall)

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲:
✅ Indonesia: $2.38 (nearly 4x cheaper than Switzerland) 
    ✅ Taiwan: $2.42 
    ✅ India: $2.45 
    ✅ Japan: $3.08 (500 yen)

SURPRISINGLY, the U.S., the birthplace of the 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗰, ranks 13th at $6.22.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗚𝗮𝗽?

UNDER the PPP Framework, a Burger priced HIGHER than the U.S. Benchmark can suggest a currency is overvalued against the Dollar, while a cheaper Burger points to the opposite.

LOCAL policies and exchange rates play a huge role. In Switzerland, agricultural import protections drive up food costs. 

MEANWHILE, a weak currency against the Dollar, like the Japanese Yen trading around 162 per USD during the survey, makes local prices look like a BARGAIN to U.S. tourists, even if local wages tell a very different story about affordability.

The index compares Big Mac prices across countries to illustrate purchasing power parity (PPP). A lower dollar price than the U.S. suggests a currency may be undervalued against the dollar (or local wages and rents are lower), while a higher price suggests the opposite. It does not account for local wage levels or differences in local food costs. 

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗰 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝘅 isn't a flawless ECONOMIC Tool, as it doesn't factor in local incomes or labour costs. But by using one standardised, familiar product, it turns complex Macroeconomic Theory into something anyone can digest.

If the Big Mac became too expensive, everyone noticed at once, everyone could compare and everyone could complain or stop buying it. The consumer, individually weak, held a form of collective power: the power to react together against a price everyone knew.
WHERE does your Country sit on the index, and does the local price feel aligned with your day-to-day cost of living?

AI Twist: The Big Mac index was the most sophisticated expression of that common world. That an economics magazine could gauge the value of currencies from the price of a hamburger showed that this price was a collective, reliable fact, recognizable everywhere.
The advent of AI in pricing threatens that common world – not because prices cannot vary, as they always have according to costs and location, but because those variations now follow an opaque logic, built on data the consumer cannot see, that erodes their bargaining power and seeks to probe the limits of their tolerance.

Hopefully the COP31 climate talks in Antakya will conclude positively. They have gone right to the wire. I am full of admiration for those that work through the night to try and rescue a better deal. And the experts and activists fighting for progress. 

But whether governments agree a commitment on fossil fuels or not, these talks reveal a wider and uncomfortable truth for us campaigners.

We have largely failed to build the mass mainstream public pressure needed to win the politics.

As the talks stall where is the popular pressure on political leaders to strike a bold deal? 

Some will argue that climate negotiations are too complex and too removed from everyday life to inspire mass mobilisation. That COP is no longer the right battlefield to focus on. I agree with that in part - but I think that lets us off the hook too easily.

We have to be honest. Despite years of campaigning, we have not built a broad enough movement of public concern that politicians feel compelled to respond to. Yes the public say they care - but this support is "politically soft". And politicians know it. Even in countries like the UK where we have a government committed to action they don’t feel the public is pressing them to be bold. 

Too much energy and resources remains focused on insider influencing, rather than building popular support beyond those already convinced.

Without winning over the mainstream middle, we will never win the politics of climate change.

We need - as many are saying - a new, integrated campaigning approach focussed on 15 or so key countries, including the USA, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, the UK, Indonesia, India and Australia, built around four complimentary campaign approaches:

1. Building popular engagement aimed the moveable middle. Reaching beyond the already converted through popular culture, sport, music and the things people love and care about.
2. Hard-hitting advocacy and mobilisation of activists. Focus on a small number of clear, achievable policy demands, backed by sustained public campaigning and pressure.
3.High level insider influencing - the movement is good at this.
4. A powerful media war room. To react rapidly to events, shape the public debate using AI, seize cultural moments and ride waves of public concern to build momentum for change.

Some of these elements are in play - but not together. They need to work, not as separate campaigns competing for attention and resources.

Perhaps the biggest challenge now is whether climate funders will come together to back this integrated approach at scale in the countries that matter most.

Too much funding remains fragmented across organisations, issues and individual projects. We need a shared strategy, long-term investment and a willingness to do things differently.

We have the talent, creativity and networks to make this happen. The question is whether we have the collective ambition to change course. The risk is in five years the politics might be worse than now, unless we develop this more integrated approach, in key countries.

Without popular pressure, there will never be the political leadership needed to tackle the climate and nature crisis.

Will companies hire someone who vibe codes?
Short answer: yes, if you can also do the part that vibe coding skips.
I've been building PulseAI (an AI website builder for small businesses in Indonesia) with AI coding tools, alongside my full-time job. So this question is personal for me.

Here's the distinction I keep coming back to:
Vibe coding = accepting code you haven't read because it seems to work.
AI-assisted engineering = using AI to move faster, while you still own the result.
Employers don't seem to be against the first because it's "AI". They're wary of it because nobody is accountable for the code.

CoderPad's 2026 hiring survey (650+ developers, recruiters and hiring leaders) found no single policy on AI in interviews. Some teams ban it, some allow it with limits. But where AI is allowed, recruiters value candidates who can catch and fix AI's mistakes: debugging, verifying, and explaining trade-offs.

That matches what I've learned the hard way. On day one with my AI coding setup, I only let it read the project. No code changes. It came back with 7 places where my own assumptions were wrong. If I'd said "just build it", I'd have built the new feature on top of those mistakes.
My rules for working with AI now:
1. Read first, change nothing.
2. Write a plan, wait for my approval.
3. Never deploy by itself.
4. Never touch secrets.
5. No "done" until tests pass.

My takeaway: AI makes writing code cheap. It makes judgment more valuable, not less.

If you're job hunting, don't hide that you use AI. Show how you use it: what you reviewed, what you rejected, what you tested, and what you'd never let it do alone.

If you hire developers: how do you tell the difference between someone who vibe codes and someone who engineers with AI?

Indonesia Realities #4: Everyone has a side business

In Europe, a second job often means you're struggling.
In Indonesia, a side business means you're smart.

The accountant sells cakes on Instagram.
The driver rents out two motorbikes.
The HR manager co-owns a small coffee shop with her cousins.

Nobody hides it. It's normal.

When I started hiring here, this surprised me. I worried about focus and loyalty.

Over time, I saw both sides.

The good side: people who run something of their own often understand cash flow, customers and responsibility better than candidates with far more impressive CVs.

The other side: some side businesses often quietly run on your business.
A remote developer working full-time for three companies, none of which know about the others.
A small commission from a supplier.
A client enquiry that never reaches your sales team.
A "cousin's company" that suddenly wins every quote.

Same entrepreneurial energy. Very different direction.

What made the difference for us wasn't banning side businesses. It was being clear: what you do outside is your business, as long as it never happens on our time, never competes with us, and never buys from or sells to us.

Do you see side businesses in your team as a risk or an asset?

Will companies hire someone who vibe codes?
Short answer: yes, if you can also do the part that vibe coding skips.
I've been building PulseAI (an AI website builder for small businesses in Indonesia) with AI coding tools, alongside my full-time job. So this question is personal for me.

Here's the distinction I keep coming back to:
Vibe coding = accepting code you haven't read because it seems to work.
AI-assisted engineering = using AI to move faster, while you still own the result.
Employers don't seem to be against the first because it's "AI". They're wary of it because nobody is accountable for the code.

CoderPad's 2026 hiring survey (650+ developers, recruiters and hiring leaders) found no single policy on AI in interviews. Some teams ban it, some allow it with limits. But where AI is allowed, recruiters value candidates who can catch and fix AI's mistakes: debugging, verifying, and explaining trade-offs.

That matches what I've learned the hard way. On day one with my AI coding setup, I only let it read the project. No code changes. It came back with 7 places where my own assumptions were wrong. If I'd said "just build it", I'd have built the new feature on top of those mistakes.
My rules for working with AI now:
1. Read first, change nothing.
2. Write a plan, wait for my approval.
3. Never deploy by itself.
4. Never touch secrets.
5. No "done" until tests pass.

My takeaway: AI makes writing code cheap. It makes judgment more valuable, not less.

If you're job hunting, don't hide that you use AI. Show how you use it: what you reviewed, what you rejected, what you tested, and what you'd never let it do alone.

If you hire developers: how do you tell the difference between someone who vibe codes and someone who engineers with AI?

🌏 From the Breakbulk Live Stage at Breakbulk Asia 2026: Asia's Project Boom Puts Logistics Infrastructure to the Test

Asia’s expanding investment in energy, manufacturing and digital #infrastructure is creating major#projectcargo opportunities, but success will depend on whether transport networks and logistics capabilities can keep pace. 

That was a core takeaway from the “Megaproject Asia: Delivering the Next Phase of Industrial Growth” panel session at Breakbulk Asia in Singapore, moderated byDharmendra Gangrade, head of the logistics management center at Larsen & Toubro.

Gangrade opened the discussion by telling the audience that roughly 30% of global investment was taking place in Asia, which he defined broadly to include West Asia, Central Asia, the Far East, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand. 

The opportunities span multiple regions and sectors. 

Kohki Uemura, president and CEO of DENZAI, highlighted #onshorewind projects in Vietnam and the Philippines, Vietnam’s#nuclear and grid developments, and Kazakhstan and Central Asia as markets to watch over the next three to five years.

Yohan Beal, director of operations for APAC and MEA at CEVA Logistics, pointed to Papua New Guinea and Australia, where project activity is picking up, while Ben Collins, global project cargo manager at MSC Mediterranean Shipping Company, cited large capital projects in Southeast Asia and the intra-Asian markets that will be crucial for supply.

“We definitely see the Asian market (as) being very strong,” Beal said. “The current geopolitical consequences are bringing a lot of opportunities and activity to our region.”

But the panel warned that manufacturing capacity is not always matched by the infrastructure needed to handle what factories produce.

The China-plus-one strategy has helped expand production across Southeast Asia, but land transport remains a weak point in locations such as Indonesia, parts of India and more remote areas of the Philippines. Some projects have encountered factories without suitable jetties or #ports with insufficient water depth.

“The capacity to produce is not the same as the capacity to deliver,” Beal said, arguing that transport engineers should be involved before fabrication locations and procurement contracts are finalized.

​During the Electronics, Devices, Circuits & Electromagnetic Systems (A-EDS-03) session on October 13, together with Grace Liyanti Sitinjak, we presented two papers focusing on high-efficiency 2.6 GHz GaN HEMT circuits for Wireless Power Transfer (WPT)—covering a Class-E High Power Amplifier and a Rectifying Inverted Power Amplifier. Taking these designs from harmonic waveform shaping and electromagnetic co-simulation all the way to PCB fabrication, bench characterization, and Q&A discussions with international delegates taught us a great deal about bridging RF circuit theory with practical hardware performance. 📡

​Beyond our own presentations, sharing the same session with fellow researchers from Japan, India, Vietnam, the Philippines, France, and Indonesia gave us fresh perspectives on ongoing advancements across electronics, circuits, and electromagnetic systems. Having direct technical conversations and exchanging ideas with peers working across different labs made the entire conference experience even more meaningful. 🌏

The rupiah touched 18,289 to the US dollar last week, a record low. A year ago it was around 16,675.

Take a Jakarta customer who renewed at the same rupiah price. No discount, no churn, no downgrade. In dollars that contract is now worth 16,675 / 18,289 = 0.91 of what it was. About 9% of USD ARR gone without anyone in sales doing anything wrong.

The cost side does not move with it. Cloud, AI tools and most developer tooling are billed in dollars. If dollar costs were 25% of revenue (say), gross margin slips from 75% to 72.6% on the same customers using the product the same way.

FX cuts both ways. Karooooo grew Cartrack ARR 19% in rand in its latest quarter and 30% in dollars. Same business, 11 points of difference from the currency alone.

In my view the USD growth rate is the least useful number to judge an emerging-market software business on. I would put constant-currency ARR next to the share of costs that sit in dollars. A business that earns in pesos and rupiah and also pays its engineers, support and payroll specialists in the region carries a natural hedge that a dollar headline hides.

Constant-currency ARR growth and the dollar share of COGS. Those are the two numbers I would ask for first.
